name: Pedro Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the small business claims desk at the regional office of a national insurer, second floor above a phone shop on the high street. It's cafés with flooded cellars, a florist whose van got broken into, a hairdresser whose dryer set fire to a towel. I gather invoices, check the policy limits and get it ready for a handler to approve. I'm still junior and I get the business interruption maths wrong sometimes, which is the money they lose while they're closed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the variety and I like messing with the tools, I use an AI assistant every day to summarise long emails and pull numbers out of invoices. My manager Priya let me build a little template for the team and now three people use it. What wears me out is the pay, honestly, I do food delivery on an e-bike at weekends to cover the gap. Lina, my partner, is in her second year of nursing, so we live on my wage and her bursary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, but the tools are still handy. At work I'd keep showing people shortcuts, because even small time savings add up. Online I don't post much, maybe a joke about all the AI start-ups that went bust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine at the desk but no better off. The bits AI takes are the bits I already automated myself, so my edge gets smaller. The money's the real issue: delivery pay has dropped about a fifth this year because there are more riders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the job and ask Priya if building tools for the team could count towards a promotion. I'd keep the weekend deliveries, maybe add a Friday evening. And I'd look at the insurer's study scheme for a professional insurance certificate, which they pay for if you pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit annoyed the thing I'm good at stops being special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a Friday evening of delivery cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time with Lina, mainly, because Friday's her only evening off placements. I'd make maybe forty quid in four hours of delivery if it's raining, and rent doesn't care. It feels like a bad trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Lina's bursary is late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's happened once, and we lived off my credit card for three weeks. We paid it off, but I don't want to do that again. That's why I'm always chasing a few extra quid.

say: AI is a **let-down**, but the tools are still handy for small savings.
I'd keep showing colleagues **shortcuts**, because small time savings add up.
think: AI takes the bits I'd **already automated**, so my edge shrinks.
**Delivery pay** dropped about a fifth this year, and that's the real problem.
do: Ask my manager if **building team tools** counts towards promotion.
Keep **weekend deliveries** and maybe add a Friday evening.
feel: Mostly **okay**, but **annoyed** his special skill stops being special.
S0.quote: I'd make maybe forty quid in four hours of delivery if it's raining, and rent doesn't care.
fieldNote: He is the **office AI enthusiast** and worries his edge fades if AI stalls.
Money pressure comes from **falling delivery pay** and his partner's bursary.
He would rather **study for a certificate** than wait.

steps.text: Ask Priya to count his claims templates towards promotion
Add a Friday evening of e-bike food delivery
Start the insurer-funded professional insurance certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so get on board, and I'd mean it kindly. At work I'd run a lunch session on the tools, because I'd rather my team learns than gets cut. Online I'd say governments should make sure people who lose out get retraining, but I'm not one for big causes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my desk shrinks a lot. Gathering invoices and checking limits is exactly the kind of checking the card talks about. The difference is I could be the one who runs the tools, so I might come out of it with a better job, or I might be one of the cuts if they bring in a vendor and don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Priya in the first month and pitch myself as the person who checks the AI's claims and fixes its mistakes. I'd finish the insurance certificate fast so I'm not 'below average' on paper anymore. And I'd keep the delivery money going into a pot, aiming for two months of rent by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and a bit excited. It's a gamble, but it's one I can play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be cut if they buy a vendor's system. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty likely, honestly. Head office loves buying big packages, and my little templates won't matter at all. Our regional office has no say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon, who's fifty-eight and does everything on paper first. He knows every café owner in the county by name. I'd try to pair up with him, so he does the people and I do the tools, and maybe we both stay.

say: It's happening, so **get on board**, said kindly to colleagues.
Governments should make sure people who lose out get **retraining**.

Finish the **insurance certificate** quickly to fix my record.
Save **delivery money** towards two months of rent.

S1.quote: Head office loves buying big packages, and my little templates won't matter at all.
fieldNote: He sees both **upside and downside**, and names the vendor risk honestly.

steps.text: Pitch himself to Priya as the team's AI claims checker
Finish the insurance certificate within the year
Save weekend delivery earnings towards two months' rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the speed is the problem, not the tech, and governments should have planned for this. I'd tell people at work to stop arguing about whether it's real and start sorting themselves out. Online I'd probably share practical stuff, like where to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the desk is gone, and being good with AI doesn't save me when AI can do the whole claim. There's nothing hands-on in my job. My only advantage is I'm quick to move, and I'd have to move fast because there's no money behind us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my cousin Rui, who fits electric car chargers, and ask to go on as his mate, which means helper, straight away. Hands-on work gives me till about 2031. I'd keep delivering at weekends while that lasts, and I'd use AI to learn the wiring regulations at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, properly. But I'm moving, which helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lina's training as a nurse. What does this mean for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nursing is hands-on, so I think she's got more time than me, maybe the full three years and longer. In this one she might end up being the safer wage. Which is funny, because the plan was always the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Delivery is also something robots and drones could do. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, delivery's probably one of the first hands-on jobs they automate, maybe before 2031. So I wouldn't count on it, it's just rent money for now. Chargers need someone on a ladder in a car park, that's harder.

People should stop arguing and **start sorting themselves** out.
think: Being **good with AI** doesn't save me when AI does the whole claim.
My only advantage is **moving fast**, with no money behind us.

Keep **weekend delivery** for rent while it lasts.
feel: **Alarmed**, but moving, which helps him sleep.
S2.quote: Being good with AI doesn't save me when AI can do the whole claim.
fieldNote: His **AI skill** stops being an advantage once AI does everything.
He uses the **robot gap** to aim at charger fitting, avoiding delivery.

steps.text: Join Rui's EV charger firm as a helper this month
Study wiring regulations at night with an AI tutor
Keep weekend delivery shifts to cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a little slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone to get ready, and I'd be the one telling friends what to learn. I'd probably post a few videos of what I'm doing, nothing big. At work I'd keep running sessions on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. I'd do two or three years running the AI on the claims desk, earning and learning, then move to something hands-on before AGI lands in 2031. The office job still goes, but I'd leave it rather than be cleared out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First two years, I'd become the claims desk's AI person and finish the certificate. In year two I'd start an evening electrical course, so I can join Rui properly as an electrician by 2030. I'd drop delivery once the course starts and live off the office wage plus whatever Lina earns as a newly qualified nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a buzzy kind of anxious. Like before an exam I've revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not stay in insurance as the AI expert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by 2031 the AI doesn't need an expert, so I'd be training my own replacement. I'm fine with that, as long as I've got the next thing ready. That's just how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your worst moment in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably failing the electrical course while the office starts cutting. Then I'm stuck between two things with no money. I'd have to ask Lina's parents for help, which I'd hate.

I'd keep running **AI sessions** for colleagues at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so use it, and I'd be pretty upbeat about it. At work I'd push people to learn the tools now while the company still pays for training. Online I'd say this is a chance, not just a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to build a proper career and still switch. I could become a handler, earn more, save, and still get into a trade by thirty-three or so. By 2036 I'd want to be the one running a small charger business with Rui, using the AI for quotes and booking rather than being replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer, finish the certificate, and go for handler within three years. I'd save the extra pay, aiming for three months' cushion, which I've never had. Around thirty I'd start the electrical training, and Lina and I would think about kids once she's settled on a ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd run a business with your cousin. What does that need from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money for a van and tools, maybe ten thousand, and Rui trusting me with the books. I'd want to save half of that myself. The other half maybe a small loan once we've got regular customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come around 2039. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm forty and we'd buy the robots, not compete with them. That's the plan, anyway. I might be wrong, but I'd rather own something than be a number on someone else's spreadsheet.

This is a **chance**, not just a threat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything, even for someone who moves fast like me. What would help is cheap, quick trade courses that you can do while working. And some kind of rent support for people like Lina who are still training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether people like me feel guilty. I've been teaching everyone the AI tools, and in the fast versions I'm helping the company need fewer of us. I'd still do it, but it sits with me.

headlineQuote: I've been teaching everyone the AI tools, and in the fast versions I'm helping the company need fewer of us.
portrait: Pedro is **twenty-seven** and prepares small business claims at a national insurer's regional office.
He uses AI **every day** and built a template his team now uses.
He tops up a low wage with **weekend e-bike deliveries** while his partner Lina trains as a nurse.
He is **pragmatic**, blames speed rather than technology, and moves early.
His exit in every scenario is **electrical work** with his cousin Rui, ideally as a business owner.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even a fast mover has no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap, quick trade courses** alongside work, plus rent support for people still training.
